header: 2026-03-04 07:12 PST · 38 min · Alex Chen, Priya Kapoor · Rachel Lin, Marcus Doyle, Sara Gomez
transcript:
00:00 Alex Chen: Hey everyone, quick hello, thanks for hopping on. I'm Alex from Redwood Inference, AE on the account, with Priya our solutions engineer. Good morning Rachel, Marcus, Sara.
00:06 Rachel Lin: Morning Alex, thanks. Excited to see the hosted API and how streaming might help our checkout chat flows.
00:10 Marcus Doyle: Hi, quick note — we care a lot about tail latency, and cost since this is high-volume. We'll probably start hosted but want an idea of dedicated later.
00:18 Priya Kapoor: Totally, we'll cover latency vs cost tradeoffs. Today I'll demo chat and text generation basics: streaming behavior, core params like temperature, max_tokens, top_p, stop sequences, and then retry/backoff patterns.
00:33 Alex Chen: Also we'll show the Console briefly and Optimize suggestions — batching and caching can cut unit cost.
00:40 Rachel Lin: Cool. For context, we expect 200 qps at peak per region, most requests are short prompts (user messages + 100 token context). We need about ~300ms p95 ideally.
00:55 Priya Kapoor: Got it. That helps. Quick architecture note: Hosted API handles streaming over HTTP/1.1 chunked transfer and also via our SDK websockets for long-lived connections, we return partial tokens as they generate.
01:10 Sara Gomez: How deterministic is the streaming? If a connection drops mid-stream, do you resume or do we need to re-request?
01:18 Priya Kapoor: Good question. Currently, hosted streaming is stateless per request — if the connection drops you re-issue the request. We recommend using an idempotency key and our recommended retry logic. For long responses we also support resume tokens in our private deployment, but for hosted we typically do simple retries with exonential backoff and token-level dedup on your side.
01:38 Marcus Doyle: Can you give an example of retry policy? We need to avoid double-charging or double-effects in the app.
01:44 Priya Kapoor: Sure. Example: on network or 5xx errors, retry up to 3 times with exponential backoff starting at 200ms, 500ms, 1s. Use idempotency-key header per user request so server can detect duplicates. For side-effectful calls (like creating orders) do server-side reconciliation or use two-phase commits. We'll share sample code in the repo.
02:10 Alex Chen: We'll put the retry patterns and sample curl and SDK snippets in the follow-up.
02:14 Rachel Lin: Great. Show us streaming demo.
02:16 Priya Kapoor: Alright demo time — I'm going to call the chat endpoint with streaming enabled, here's the payload: model: redwood-chat-1, messages: system + user, temperature: 0.2, max_tokens: 150, stream: true. I'm using our node SDK but the curl example is basically curl -N with chunked response.
02:36 Priya (screen): You can see streaming events come in every ~40-80ms depending on token generation. The SDK exposes an on('data') callback for partial chunks. If you prefer raw HTTP, we also return SSE-like events.
02:50 Sara Gomez: Are streaming chunks aligned to tokens or phrases?
02:54 Priya Kapoor: They are roughly token-aligned. We buffer a small amount to avoid tiny packets, so sometimes you'll get multiple tokens in a chunk. For latency-sensitive apps you can tune the chunk_size_hint at the model level — we'll help tune that in POC.
03:14 Marcus Doyle: What about parameters — temperature and top_p — what's safe for us? We need consistent, low-regression replies for checkout guidance.
03:21 Priya Kapoor: For deterministic outputs keep temperature low (0-0.2) and consider top_p ~0.8-1.0, plus set stop sequences to cut off after known tokens. For high-accuracy you can also use logit_bias to reduce bad completions. We can run evals on your prompt set to recommend the best config.
03:40 Rachel Lin: How do you handle token limits? We have a lot of metadata in context.
03:44 Priya Kapoor: We recommend client-side trimming and also using prefix/KV cache for repeated system instructions to reduce tokens. Hosted API supports per-call max_tokens and overall request length limits; we'll surface model token budgets in the Console. Optimize will suggest quantization or model variants if cost becomes main concern.
04:05 Alex Chen: Quick Console peek — here's the per-route latency and cost breakdown, token-level billing, and an example route with streaming enabled. You can set quotas and rate limits per API key.
04:22 Rachel Lin: Ok nice. On security, we need SOC2 plus SSO and audit logs. How's Redwood on that?
04:28 Alex Chen: We're SOC2 Type II; we support SAML/SSO, RBAC, and audit logs in the Console. For hosted we encrypt at rest and in transit and integrate with KMS for enterprise accounts. We'll share the security pack.
04:41 Marcus Doyle: Data residency? We have EU customers, need EU-only processing.
04:45 Alex Chen: Hosted has region selection for data residency; for strict requirements we offer Private (VPC) deployments. We'll include options and estimated timelines.
04:55 Sara Gomez: Back to retries — do you return a request_id in each streamed chunk so we can correlate logs?
04:59 Priya Kapoor: Yes each response includes request_id header; chunk envelopes include chunk_id and cumulative token offsets in the response metadata. Note: sometimes ASR of names in the transcript may be off — but that's just the call recording.
05:16 Rachel Lin: Do you have client-side examples for exponential backoff?
05:19 Priya Kapoor: Yes, node/python/Go examples. We'll include a snippet: retry for transient errors (502,503,504), max_retries 3, backoff factor 2, jitter to avoid thundering herd. Also show idempotency-key header usage.
05:35 Marcus Doyle: Pricing — can you ballpark token cost for hosted vs dedicated?
05:38 Alex Chen: Ballpark only in call: hosted per-token bill + throughput-based discounts as you scale; dedicated turns into reserved capacity with lower per-token compute cost but a monthly commit. I'll send an apples-to-apples comparison in the follow-up.
05:52 Rachel Lin: For the POC we'd like to run a short benchmark with our prompts and 1k sample conversations. Can Redwood run that or should we spin up env?
05:59 Priya Kapoor: We can run it in the sandbox; best is you provide a sanitized sample dataset and we'll run with your traffic profile. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 and cost estimates. Priya to own setup, Marcus to provide sample.
06:10 Sara Gomez: Any known gotchas with streaming and timeouts on mobile clients?
06:14 Priya Kapoor: Mobile clients can have connection drops; we recommend short keepalives and graceful fallbacks — show partial response to user and re-request missing portion with idempotency keys if server supports resume (on private deployments). For hosted we do reconnect+retry.
06:30 Alex Chen: We'll also send guidance for batching small requests — sometimes batching at the network edge helps throughput but increases latency; Optimize will suggest batching window sizes and caching rules that match your latency SLO.
06:44 Rachel Lin: About SDKs — are there official Ruby and PHP libs? Our app stack has some legacy PHP.
06:49 Alex Chen: Official SDKs: Node, Python, Go, Java; community SDKs exist for Ruby/PHP — we can share community links and code samples. The REST API is language-agnostic.
06:58 Marcus Doyle: Any sandbox quotas? We need to stress test.
07:02 Priya Kapoor: Sandbox has a credit bump for POC customers — we'll enlarge the quota for the benchmark run.
07:06 Rachel Lin: Great. Last question — how do you handle model rollouts and regressions?
07:10 Alex Chen: We do canary rollouts and A/B experiments per model version, and Redwood Optimize tracks quality regressions tied to your eval prompt set. If a new model drops quality we can automatically rollback routes.
07:25 Rachel Lin: Perfect. Thanks.
07:27 Alex Chen: Recap of next steps... we'll send pricing/security pack, Priya will run benchmark, Marcus will share sample data. Any other questions?
07:34 Marcus Doyle: Nope, that's it. Thanks.
07:36 Rachel Lin: Thanks Alex, Priya.
07:37 Alex Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up by Friday.
07:38 End of call.
